--- title: "Solid Waste and Network Models" subtitle: "Lecture 18" author: "Vivek Srikrishnan" course: "BEE 4750" institution: "Cornell University" date: "November 09, 2026" format: revealjs: slide-number: c/t show-slide-number: all center-title-slide: true width: 1280 height: 720 transition: none toc: true toc-depth: 1 toc-title: "Overview" history: false link-external-newwindow: true theme: ../sass/slides.scss template-partials: - title-slide.html menu: numbers: true html-math-method: mathjax include-in-header: mathjax-config.html date-format: long email-obfuscation: javascript chalkboard: theme: whiteboard buttons: true controls: true engine: julia julia: exeflags: ["+1.11.5"] execute: freeze: auto daemon: 600 --- # Review of Last Class ## Indicator Variables and Mixed Integer Programming Binary decisions need **indicator variables** $u \in \{0, 1\}$: - changes decision problem to **mixed integer**; - write **conditional** constraints or objectives using indicators; - basic solution algorithm is **branch and bound**. ## Questions? :::: {.columns .center} ::: {.column width="40%"} ![](figures/vsrikrish-poll.png){fig-alt="Poll Everywhere QR Code" fig-align="center" width="100%"} ::: ::: {.column width=60%} **Text**: VSRIKRISH to 22333 **URL**: [https://pollev.com/vsrikrish](https://pollev.com/vsrikrish)

[See Results](https://www.polleverywhere.com/multiple_choice_polls/qKeig0hHShZYHAOmvZtZm?preview=true&controls=none){preview-link="true"} ::: :::: # Solid Waste Management ## Waste Load Allocation :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width=50%} Some relevant questions: - Where do we send waste? - What types of facilities do we build/operate? ::: ::: {.column width=50%} ![Waste Management Hierarchy](https://www.epa.gov/sites/default/files/styles/medium/public/2015-08/hierarchy_hierarchy_and_options_pages.png){width=100%} ::: {.caption} Source: [EPA](https://www.epa.gov/homeland-security-waste/waste-management-options-homeland-security-incidents) ::: ::: :::: ::: {.notes} Waste management options form a hierarchy: reduce first, then recycle, then recover energy, and landfill last. There are a variety of types of facilities, and a waste management plan requires deciding which facilities to build or operate. ::: ## Waste Allocation As A Network Waste moves as *flows* between waste sources and sinks (disposal sites) based on transportation networks. ![Network Representation](figures/waste-network-blank.svg){width=75%} ::: {.notes} A network has nodes and edges. We want to decide how to allocate waste given the restrictions of the road network as well as processing any residual waste. ::: ## Network and Decision Parameterization :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width=50%} ![Network Parameterization](figures/waste-network-params.svg) ::: ::: {.column width=50%} | Variable | Definition | | :--: | :------- | | $\color{purple}S_i$ | Waste produced at source $i$ (Mg/day) | | $\color{red}K_j$ | Capacity of disposal $j$ (Mg/day) | | $\color{blue}W_{ij}$ | Waste transported from source $i$ to disposal $j$ (Mg/day) | ::: :::: ## Conservation at Each Node **Mass balance** holds at each facility: - A waste source does not hold onto any waste, $\sum_j W_{ij} = S_i$, - Incoming flows at a disposal facility have to balance with waste disposal and outflows of residual waste (*e.g.* material that cannot be recycled). # Waste Management Example ## Example System :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width=60%} ![Waste Management Example](figures/waste-example-network.svg) ::: ::: {.column width=40%} Three disposal options: - Waste-to-Energy (WTE) - Materials Recovery Facility (MRF) - Landfill (LF) ::: :::: ::: {.notes} Two cities, producing 100 and 170 Mg/day, and three facilities with the capacities in red. Distances in blue. ::: ## Example System :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width=60%} ![Waste Management Example](figures/waste-example-network.svg) ::: ::: {.column width=40%} We do not have to operate all facilities. The MRF and WTE reduce waste mass but create residuals which must be further disposed of. ::: :::: ::: {.notes} Note the edges between facilities: the MRF sends its residual to the WTE or the landfill, and the WTE sends its ash to the landfill. ::: ## Decision Variables ***What are our decision variables?*** ::: {.fragment .fade-in} Variable | Definition :--: | :----- $W_{ij}$ | Waste transported from city $i$ to disposal $j$ (Mg/day) $R_{kj}$ | Residual waste transported from disposal $k$ to disposal $j$ (Mg/day) $Y_j$ | Operational status (on/off) of disposal $j$ (binary) ::: ## Objective: Minimize Costs - **Transportation**: transporting waste has a per-weight cost $a_{ij}$ (\$/Mg-km) times the distance $l_{ij}$ (km). - **Disposal**: facilities have a fixed cost to operate $c_j$ (\$/day) and a variable tipping cost $b_j$ (\$/Mg). $$\begin{aligned} Y_j &= \begin{cases}0 & \text{if facility } j \text{ is not operated} \\ 1 & \text{if facility } j \text{ is operated} \end{cases}\\ \text{Disposal cost} &= \sum_j \left[c_j \, Y_j + b_j \times (\text{everything arriving at } j)\right] \end{aligned}$$ ## Costs For Our Problem | Facility | Fixed cost (\$/yr) | Fixed cost (\$/day) | Tipping (\$/Mg) | Capacity (Mg/day) | |:--|--:|--:|--:|--:| | WTE (1) | 900,000 | 2,466 | 60 | 150 | | MRF (2) | 400,000 | 1,096 | 5 | 130 | | LF (3) | 700,000 | 1,918 | 40 | 200 | Transport costs \$1\.50/Mg-km. The MRF recycles 40% of what it receives, at \$35/Mg recycled, and passes on the rest; the WTE leaves 20% of its input as ash. ::: {.notes} The daily fixed costs are the annual costs divided by 365. The MRF is cheap to run but the 60% it does not recycle still has to go to the WTE or the landfill. ::: ## Calculating the Objective The objective adds up each facility's fixed cost, the tipping on what arrives (and, at the MRF, the recycling cost), and the hauling, **e.g. for the MRF**: $$ \begin{aligned} & \underbrace{1{,}096\,Y_2}_{\text{fixed cost}} + \underbrace{(5 + 0.4 \times 35)\,(W_{12} + W_{22})}_{\text{tipping and recycling}} \\ & + \underbrace{1.5\,(5\,W_{12} + 15\,W_{22})}_{\text{hauling in}} + \underbrace{1.5\,(15\,R_{21} + 32\,R_{23})}_{\text{hauling its residual out}} \\[0.6em] & = 1{,}096\,Y_2 + 26.5\,W_{12} + 41.5\,W_{22} + 22.5\,R_{21} + 48\,R_{23} \end{aligned} $$ ## Mass Balance for Sources and Residuals :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width=45%} Outflows from cities have to match produced waste: $W_{11} + W_{12} + W_{13} =$ 100 $W_{21} + W_{22} + W_{23} =$ 170 ::: ::: {.column width=55%} ::: {.fragment .fade-in} Facilities can produce residual waste (outflows after processing): WTE ash: $$R_{13} = 0.2\,(W_{11} + W_{21} + R_{21})$$ MRF residual: $$R_{21} + R_{23} = 0.6\,(W_{12} + W_{22})$$ ::: ::: :::: ## Capacity Constraints Need to modify capacity constraints to ensure that a closed facility receives no waste: $$ \begin{aligned} \text{WTE:}& \quad W_{11} + W_{21} + R_{21} \leq 150\,Y_1 \\ \text{MRF:}& \quad W_{12} + W_{22} \leq 130\,Y_2 \\ \text{LF:}& \quad W_{13} + W_{23} + R_{13} + R_{23} \leq 200\,Y_3 \end{aligned} $$ ## The Full Problem {.smaller} $$ \begin{aligned} \min_{\mathbf{W}, \mathbf{R}, \mathbf{Y}} \quad & 82.5\,W_{11} + 26.5\,W_{12} + 85\,W_{13} + 75\,W_{21} + 41.5\,W_{22} + 77.5\,W_{23} \\ & + 82.5\,R_{21} + 88\,R_{23} + 67\,R_{13} + 2{,}466\,Y_1 + 1{,}096\,Y_2 + 1{,}918\,Y_3 \\[0.4em] \text{subject to:} \quad & W_{11} + W_{12} + W_{13} = 100 \qquad \text{(City 1)} \\ & W_{21} + W_{22} + W_{23} = 170 \qquad \text{(City 2)} \\ & R_{13} = 0.2\,(W_{11} + W_{21} + R_{21}) \qquad \text{(WTE ash)} \\ & R_{21} + R_{23} = 0.6\,(W_{12} + W_{22}) \qquad \text{(MRF residual)} \\ & W_{11} + W_{21} + R_{21} \leq 150\,Y_1 \qquad \text{(WTE capacity)} \\ & W_{12} + W_{22} \leq 130\,Y_2 \qquad \text{(MRF capacity)} \\ & W_{13} + W_{23} + R_{13} + R_{23} \leq 200\,Y_3 \qquad \text{(LF capacity)} \\ & W_{ij},\, R_{kj} \geq 0, \quad Y_j \in \{0, 1\} \end{aligned} $$ # Solving The Problem ## The Data in Julia ```julia # The example system: two cities, three facilities (1 = WTE, 2 = MRF, 3 = LF) waste = [100, 170] # [Mg/day] produced by each city capacity = [150, 130, 200] # [Mg/day] facility capacity fixed_cost_year = [900_000, 400_000, 700_000] # [$/yr] if the facility operates fixed_cost = round.(Int, fixed_cost_year ./ 365) # [$/day] tipping = [60, 5, 40] # [$/Mg] handled at each facility recycle_rate = 0.4 # fraction of MRF input recycled recycle_cost = 35 # [$/Mg recycled] ash_rate = 0.2 # WTE input left as ash transport_rate = 1.5 # [$/Mg-km] city_distance = [15 5 30; 10 15 25] # [km] from city i to facility j mrf_to_wte, mrf_to_lf, wte_to_lf = 15, 32, 18 # [km] residual routes # Cost of sending 1 Mg from city i to facility j: haul it, tip it, and # (at the MRF) pay to recycle the fraction that is recovered city_cost = zeros(2, 3) for i in 1:2 for j in 1:3 city_cost[i, j] = transport_rate * city_distance[i, j] + tipping[j] if j == 2 city_cost[i, j] = city_cost[i, j] + recycle_rate * recycle_cost end end end cost_R21 = transport_rate * mrf_to_wte + tipping[1] # MRF residual to WTE cost_R23 = transport_rate * mrf_to_lf + tipping[3] # MRF residual to LF cost_R13 = transport_rate * wte_to_lf + tipping[3] # WTE ash to LF ``` ::: {.notes} You don't need to walk through this; it's there for student reference. ::: ## Writing the Model in JuMP ::: {#16 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code code-fold="false"} # The model as formulated on the previous slides function waste_model(; landfill_capacity=capacity[3]) cap = [capacity[1], capacity[2], landfill_capacity] model = Model(HiGHS.Optimizer) set_silent(model) @variable(model, W[1:2, 1:3] >= 0) # city i -> facility j [Mg/day] @variable(model, R21 >= 0) # MRF residual -> WTE @variable(model, R23 >= 0) # MRF residual -> LF @variable(model, R13 >= 0) # WTE ash -> LF @variable(model, Y[1:3], Bin) # facility operates? @objective(model, Min, sum(city_cost[i, j] * W[i, j] for i in 1:2, j in 1:3) + cost_R21 * R21 + cost_R23 * R23 + cost_R13 * R13 + sum(fixed_cost[j] * Y[j] for j in 1:3)) @constraint(model, city[i in 1:2], sum(W[i, :]) == waste[i]) @constraint(model, ash, R13 == ash_rate * (W[1, 1] + W[2, 1] + R21)) @constraint(model, residual, R21 + R23 == (1 - recycle_rate) * (W[1, 2] + W[2, 2])) @constraint(model, wte, W[1, 1] + W[2, 1] + R21 <= cap[1] * Y[1]) @constraint(model, mrf, W[1, 2] + W[2, 2] <= cap[2] * Y[2]) @constraint(model, lf, W[1, 3] + W[2, 3] + R13 + R23 <= cap[3] * Y[3]) return model end ``` ::: ::: {.notes} You also don't need to walk through this: they've seen the relevant parts of setting up a MILP. ::: ## Solving the Example in JuMP ``` {.julia .cell-code code-fold="true"} # The optimal flows, on/off decisions and cost of a solved model function solution(model) W, Y = model[:W], model[:Y] R21, R23, R13 = model[:R21], model[:R23], model[:R13] return (cost=objective_value(model), Y=round.(Int, value.(Y)), W=value.(W), R21=value(R21), R23=value(R23), R13=value(R13), lf_load=value(W[1, 3] + W[2, 3] + R13 + R23)) end base_model = waste_model() optimize!(base_model) base = solution(base_model) # The solution as a table println("| Solution | Value |") println("|:--|--:|") println("| Cost (\\\$/day) | ", commas(base.cost), " |") println("| \$Y\$ (WTE, MRF, LF) | ", join(base.Y, ", "), " |") println("| \$W_{1j}\$, City 1 to WTE, MRF, LF (Mg/day) | ", join(fmt.(base.W[1, :]), ", "), " |") println("| \$W_{2j}\$, City 2 to WTE, MRF, LF (Mg/day) | ", join(fmt.(base.W[2, :]), ", "), " |") println("| \$R_{21}\$, \$R_{23}\$, \$R_{13}\$ (Mg/day) | ", join(fmt.([base.R21, base.R23, base.R13]), ", "), " |") ``` | Solution | Value | |:--|--:| | Cost (\$/day) | 26,881 | | $Y$ (WTE, MRF, LF) | 1, 1, 1 | | $W_{1j}$, City 1 to WTE, MRF, LF (Mg/day) | 0, 100, 0 | | $W_{2j}$, City 2 to WTE, MRF, LF (Mg/day) | 0, 0, 170 | | $R_{21}$, $R_{23}$, $R_{13}$ (Mg/day) | 37.5, 22.5, 7.5 | ::: {.notes} Most important: Y line, where all facilities are operated. Then City 1 sends everything to the MRF, City 2 sends everything to the LF. ::: ## The Optimal Plan's Flows :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width=55%} ![Waste Management Problem Solution](figures/waste-example-solution.svg) ::: ::: {.column width=45%} | Flow | Mg/day | |:--|--:| | City 1 → MRF | 100 | | City 2 → LF | 170 | | MRF residual → WTE | 37\.5 | | MRF residual → LF | 22\.5 | | WTE ash → LF | 7\.5 | ::: :::: ::: {.notes} The MRF's residual is split between the WTE and the landfill. ::: ## Shadow Prices for a MILP - Shadow prices are not well-defined for MILPs as they are for LPs because an indicator variable can only switch between 0 and 1. - One approach: Fix the indicators at their optimal values to produce an LP with the same solution. - This LP's shadow prices are **conditional** on that choice: they describe small changes with the same facilities running. ::: {.notes} If a change is large enough that the cheapest plan opens or closes a facility, the conditional shadow price no longer describes the change in the objective (just like sufficiently large changes for LPs), because the change in fixed costs creates a discontinuity. ::: ## MIP Shadow Prices in `JuMP` ```julia optimize!(model) # the MILP: no shadow prices yet fix_discrete_variables(model) # fix each Y_j at its optimal 0 or 1 optimize!(model) # an LP with the same solution shadow_price(lf) # conditional on which facilities run ``` - By default, `JuMP` reports no shadow prices for a MILP. - `fix_discrete_variables()` fixes the indicator variables at the optimal values so the rest of the problem becomes an LP. ## Conditional Shadow Prices :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width=50%} ``` {.julia .cell-code code-fold="true"} # Fix the binaries at their optimal values and re-solve: an LP with the same solution fix_discrete_variables(base_model) optimize!(base_model) # Sizes of the shadow prices: for a city, the cost of one more Mg/day of waste; # for a facility, the saving from one more Mg/day of capacity base_price = (city=-shadow_price.(base_model[:city]), wte=-shadow_price(base_model[:wte]), mrf=-shadow_price(base_model[:mrf]), lf=-shadow_price(base_model[:lf])) # Landfill space freed per Mg moved from the landfill to the WTE: its ash comes back [Mg] space_per_Mg = 1 - ash_rate # The table's sign: + if one more Mg/day raises the cost, - if it lowers it signed(x) = x > 0.005 ? "+" * money(x) : (x < -0.005 ? "−" * money(-x) : "0.00") println("| One more Mg/day of | Change in cost (\\\$/day) |") println("|:--|--:|") println("| City 1's waste | ", signed(base_price.city[1]), " |") println("| City 2's waste | ", signed(base_price.city[2]), " |") println("| WTE capacity | ", signed(-base_price.wte), " |") println("| MRF capacity | ", signed(-base_price.mrf), " |") println("| Landfill capacity | ", signed(-base_price.lf), " |") ``` | One more Mg/day of | Change in cost (\$/day) | |:--|--:| | City 1's waste | +85.22 | | City 2's waste | +87.38 | | WTE capacity | 0.00 | | MRF capacity | 0.00 | | Landfill capacity | −9.88 | ::: ::: {.column width=10%} ::: ::: {.column width=40%} Moving 1 Mg to the WTE frees only 0\.8 Mg in the landfill. So each additional Mg/day of landfill capacity takes 1\.25 Mg/day of MRF residual away from the WTE, saving \$9\.88/day. ::: :::: ::: {.notes} The landfill's capacity is the binding constraint. Every route for new waste has to account for the full landfill. ::: ## What If the Landfill Were Expanded? ``` {.julia .cell-code code-fold="true"} bigger_capacity = 220 bigger_model = waste_model(landfill_capacity=bigger_capacity) optimize!(bigger_model) bigger = solution(bigger_model) println("| Landfill capacity (Mg/day) | Cost (\\\$/day) | WTE | MRF | LF |") println("|:--|--:|:--:|:--:|:--:|") for (lf_capacity, r) in ((capacity[3], base), (bigger_capacity, bigger)) status = fill("open", 3) for j in 1:3 if r.Y[j] == 0 status[j] = "**closed**" end end println("| ", lf_capacity, " | ", commas(r.cost), " | ", join(status, " | "), " |") end ``` | Landfill capacity (Mg/day) | Cost (\$/day) | WTE | MRF | LF | |:--|--:|:--:|:--:|:--:| | 200 | 26,881 | open | open | open | | 220 | 24,539 | **closed** | open | open | With 20 Mg/day more landfill capacity, the **WTE closes** and the system saves \$2,342/day. The landfill's shadow price predicted a saving of only 20 × \$9\.88 = \$198/day. ::: {.notes} The shadow price assumes the same facilities run and the same constraints are binding. Here the change is large enough that the WTE closes, and its fixed cost of \$2,466/day goes away, so the actual saving is far larger than the shadow price predicts. ::: # Limits on Trucking ## City 2's Trucks Suppose City 2's collection trucks also haul its waste to the facilities. We assume each carries 10 Mg, averages 40 km/h and takes 15 minutes to unload, so a load takes: | From City 2 to | Hours per load | Truck-hours per Mg | |:--|--:|--:| | WTE (10 km) | 0.75 | 0.075 | | MRF (15 km) | 1.00 | 0.100 | | LF (25 km) | 1.50 | 0.150 | ::: {.notes} A fleet's time is what usually limits how much a city can haul directly: collection trucks have to collect as well as haul, and a long trip to a distant site takes a truck off its route for longer. (Truck size, speed and unloading time are assumptions for this example; rear-loading collection trucks typically carry about 6 to 19 tons, depending on the body and how tightly the waste is compacted.) The landfill is the farthest facility from City 2, so each Mg sent there takes twice the truck time of a Mg sent to the WTE. Each load is a round trip plus unloading. ::: ## Limits on City 2's Trucking Capacity Sending all 170 Mg/day to the landfill takes 25\.5 truck-hours a day. Suppose City 2's trucks have only 24 hours. This produces a new constraint: $$0.075\,W_{21} + 0.100\,W_{22} + 0.150\,W_{23} \leq 24 \quad \text{(truck-hours/day)}$$ ::: {.notes} This is an example of a **flow constraint**: it limits outflows along City 2's edges, each weighted by how long the trip takes. ::: ## Re-Solving With the Truck Limit {.smaller} ``` {.julia .cell-code code-fold="true"} # The model as formulated, plus a limit on City 2's truck-hours [truck-hours/day] function solve_with_truck_limit(fleet_hours) model = waste_model() W = model[:W] @constraint(model, fleet, sum(hours_per_Mg[j] * W[2, j] for j in 1:3) <= fleet_hours) optimize!(model) result = solution(model) truck_hours = sum(hours_per_Mg[j] * result.W[2, j] for j in 1:3) fix_discrete_variables(model) # for the shadow price, as before optimize!(model) return merge(result, (truck_hours=truck_hours, fleet_price=-shadow_price(fleet))) end trucks = solve_with_truck_limit(fleet_limit) println("| | No limit | $(fleet_limit) truck-hours |") println("|:--|--:|--:|") println("| City 2 → WTE (Mg/day) | ", fmt(base.W[2, 1]), " | ", fmt(trucks.W[2, 1]), " |") println("| City 2 → LF (Mg/day) | ", fmt(base.W[2, 3]), " | ", fmt(trucks.W[2, 3]), " |") println("| MRF residual → WTE (Mg/day) | ", fmt(base.R21), " | ", fmt(trucks.R21), " |") println("| MRF residual → LF (Mg/day) | ", fmt(base.R23), " | ", fmt(trucks.R23), " |") println("| City 2 truck-hours/day | ", fmt(base_truck_hours), " | ", fmt(trucks.truck_hours), " |") println("| Cost (\\\$/day) | ", commas(base.cost), " | ", commas(trucks.cost), " |") ``` | | No limit | 24 truck-hours | |:--|--:|--:| | City 2 → WTE (Mg/day) | 0 | 20 | | City 2 → LF (Mg/day) | 170 | 150 | | MRF residual → WTE (Mg/day) | 37.5 | 17.5 | | MRF residual → LF (Mg/day) | 22.5 | 42.5 | | City 2 truck-hours/day | 25.5 | 24 | | Cost (\$/day) | 26,881 | 26,941 | ::: {.notes} The whole network now adjusts to the new constraint. City 2 can cut its truck time only by sending waste somewhere closer than the landfill, and the WTE is the closest. The WTE has room for City 2's waste only if it burns less of the MRF's residual, and that residual then goes to the landfill, which is still operating at full capacity. ::: ## What Is a Truck-Hour Worth? The truck limit's shadow price is **\$40\.00/day per truck-hour**. One more truck-hour lets City 2 send 13\.3 Mg/day to the landfill instead of the WTE, saving \$3\.00 per Mg. # Key Takeaways ## Key Takeaways - A network model's decisions are **flows** on edges, constrained by **conservation** at each node. - Waste facilities can produce residuals which need to be processed or disposed of at the next level of the waste disposal hierarchy. - A **flow constraint** limits edges, not nodes, unlike mass-balance constraints. ## Network Models Elsewhere - Can have more advanced network models with highly-specified routes: - Transportation networks - Power transmission networks - Pipeline networks - Flows could also be bidirectional. # Upcoming Schedule ## Next Classes **Wednesday, November 11**: Lab 3, Fixed Costs and Facility Siting in JuMP. **Monday, November 16**: Quiz 5, then stochastic optimization and scenario trees. ## Assessments **HW8**: assigned Wednesday, due Thursday, November 19 (network models and waste allocation). **Project update**: due Friday, November 13. **Quiz 5**: Monday, November 16 (capacity expansion, mixed integer programming, and waste and network models).
